<title>Unveiling the aging-immune axis in irritable bowel syndrome: a multi-omics and machine learning approach to biomarker discovery and validation</title>
<abstract>Background Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a prevalent functional gastrointestinal disorder with an elusive pathophysiology. Although immune dysregulation and mild mucosal inflammation are recognized as important factors in IBS, the specific contribution of immunosenescence remains unclear. Prior MR studies on IBS focused on single molecular traits; however, an integrated multi−omics framework for aging−immune genes has not been applied. Here, we integrate cis−eQTL/pQTL/mQTL with machine learning and in vivo validation to identify putatively causal biomarkers and unravel the aging−immune axis. Methods Aging- and immune-related genes were curated from published databases and analyzed using genome-wide cis-expression quantitative trait loci (cis-eQTL), cis-protein quantitative trait loci (cis-pQTL), and cis-methylation quantitative trait loci (cis-mQTL) datasets. All QTL data were derived from blood or plasma samples. Candidate genes were identified through integrative multi-omics analysis, followed by functional annotation, machine learning-based feature selection, immune infiltration profiling, and drug-target prediction. The expression of key biomarkers was validated using reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) in colonic tissues from a rat model of diarrhea-predominant IBS (IBS-D). Results Integrative multi-omics analysis initially identified 34 high-confidence candidate genes. Through multi-algorithm machine learning such as least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), support vector machine recursive feature elimination (SVM-RFE), and random forest, these candidates were refined to a core panel of five biomarkers: the antioxidant enzyme catalase (CAT), acyl-CoA dehydrogenase very long chain (ACADVL), chemokine (C-C motif) ligand 4 (CCL4), cyclin E1 (CCNE1), and Jagged canonical Notch ligand 1 (JAG1). These biomarkers demonstrated strong diagnostic performance for CAT, CCNE1, and JAG1 in the validation cohort (AUC: 0.935–0.951), while ACADVL and CCL4 showed only moderate diagnostic potential (AUC: 0.645–0.649). The combined AUC range in the training cohort was 0.898–0.959. However, in the IBS-D rat model, only JAG1 was significantly upregulated in colonic tissue, whereas CAT, ACADVL, CCL4, and CCNE1 showed no significant changes. Among the five markers, only JAG1 was significantly upregulated in the IBS-D rat colon, confirming its local gut relevance. CAT and CCNE1 showed strong diagnostic performance (AUC >0.9), whereas ACADVL and CCL4 performed modestly (AUC <0.7). Given the blood-derived QTL data and colonic validation, cross-tissue heterogeneity is a key caveat: JAG1 is robustly validated in colon, while the remaining four markers—especially ACADVL and CCL4—require further evaluation in blood, PBMCs, or other relevant tissues. Functional enrichment analysis revealed their involvement in critical biological processes, including oxidative stress, fatty acid metabolism, immune cell recruitment, cell cycle progression, and epithelial-immune crosstalk via Notch signaling. Immune infiltration analysis uncovered a distinct immune landscape in IBS, with significant correlations between biomarker expression and immune cell populations. Notably, only JAG1 was significantly upregulated in the colonic tissues of the IBS-D rat model, confirming its relevance to gut pathophysiology. No significant changes were detected for CAT, ACADVL, CCL4, or CCNE1 in the same tissue samples, highlighting the tissue-specific nature of these candidate biomarkers. The SMR analysis demonstrated consistent causal directions between genetically predicted expression and disease risk for these five markers, with no discordance relative to their upregulation in IBS patients. All biomarker validation was performed at the transcriptomic level (RT−qPCR); no protein−level assays (e.g., Western blot, IHC, or ELISA) were conducted. Conclusions This study delineates the genetic architecture linking aging and immunity to IBS through an integrative multi−omics and machine learning approach, providing novel putatively causal evidence and identifying JAG1 as a robustly validated biomarker with diagnostic and therapeutic potential. The remaining candidates warrant further investigation in appropriate biological contexts.</abstract>
</record>

<title>Unveiling the aging-immune axis in irritable bowel syndrome: a multi-omics and machine learning approach to biomarker discovery and validation</title>
<abstract>Background Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a prevalent functional gastrointestinal disorder with an elusive pathophysiology. Although immune dysregulation and mild mucosal inflammation are recognized as important factors in IBS, the specific contribution of immunosenescence remains unclear. Prior MR studies on IBS focused on single molecular traits; however, an integrated multi−omics framework for aging−immune genes has not been applied. Here, we integrate cis−eQTL/pQTL/mQTL with machine learning and in vivo validation to identify putatively causal biomarkers and unravel the aging−immune axis. Methods Aging- and immune-related genes were curated from published databases and analyzed using genome-wide cis-expression quantitative trait loci (cis-eQTL), cis-protein quantitative trait loci (cis-pQTL), and cis-methylation quantitative trait loci (cis-mQTL) datasets. All QTL data were derived from blood or plasma samples. Candidate genes were identified through integrative multi-omics analysis, followed by functional annotation, machine learning-based feature selection, immune infiltration profiling, and drug-target prediction. The expression of key biomarkers was validated using reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) in colonic tissues from a rat model of diarrhea-predominant IBS (IBS-D). Results Integrative multi-omics analysis initially identified 34 high-confidence candidate genes. Through multi-algorithm machine learning such as least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), support vector machine recursive feature elimination (SVM-RFE), and random forest, these candidates were refined to a core panel of five biomarkers: the antioxidant enzyme catalase (CAT), acyl-CoA dehydrogenase very long chain (ACADVL), chemokine (C-C motif) ligand 4 (CCL4), cyclin E1 (CCNE1), and Jagged canonical Notch ligand 1 (JAG1). These biomarkers demonstrated strong diagnostic performance for CAT, CCNE1, and JAG1 in the validation cohort (AUC: 0.935–0.951), while ACADVL and CCL4 showed only moderate diagnostic potential (AUC: 0.645–0.649). The combined AUC range in the training cohort was 0.898–0.959. However, in the IBS-D rat model, only JAG1 was significantly upregulated in colonic tissue, whereas CAT, ACADVL, CCL4, and CCNE1 showed no significant changes. Among the five markers, only JAG1 was significantly upregulated in the IBS-D rat colon, confirming its local gut relevance. CAT and CCNE1 showed strong diagnostic performance (AUC >0.9), whereas ACADVL and CCL4 performed modestly (AUC <0.7). Given the blood-derived QTL data and colonic validation, cross-tissue heterogeneity is a key caveat: JAG1 is robustly validated in colon, while the remaining four markers—especially ACADVL and CCL4—require further evaluation in blood, PBMCs, or other relevant tissues. Functional enrichment analysis revealed their involvement in critical biological processes, including oxidative stress, fatty acid metabolism, immune cell recruitment, cell cycle progression, and epithelial-immune crosstalk via Notch signaling. Immune infiltration analysis uncovered a distinct immune landscape in IBS, with significant correlations between biomarker expression and immune cell populations. Notably, only JAG1 was significantly upregulated in the colonic tissues of the IBS-D rat model, confirming its relevance to gut pathophysiology. No significant changes were detected for CAT, ACADVL, CCL4, or CCNE1 in the same tissue samples, highlighting the tissue-specific nature of these candidate biomarkers. <abstract>Background Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a prevalent functional gastrointestinal disorder with an elusive pathophysiology. Although immune dysregulation and mild mucosal inflammation are recognized as important factors in IBS, the specific contribution of immunosenescence remains unclear. Prior MR studies on IBS focused on single molecular traits; however, an integrated multi−omics framework for aging−immune genes has not been applied. Here, we integrate cis−eQTL/pQTL/mQTL with machine learning and in vivo validation to identify putatively causal biomarkers and unravel the aging−immune axis. All QTL data were derived from blood or plasma samples. Candidate genes were identified through integrative multi-omics analysis, followed by functional annotation, machine learning-based feature selection, immune infiltration profiling, and drug-target prediction. The expression of key biomarkers was validated using reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) in colonic tissues from a rat model of diarrhea-predominant IBS (IBS-D). Results Integrative multi-omics analysis initially identified 34 high-confidence candidate genes. Through multi-algorithm machine learning such as least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), support vector machine recursive feature elimination (SVM-RFE), and random forest, these candidates were refined to a core panel of five biomarkers: the antioxidant enzyme catalase (CAT), acyl-CoA dehydrogenase very long chain (ACADVL), chemokine (C-C motif) ligand 4 (CCL4), cyclin E1 (CCNE1), and Jagged canonical Notch ligand 1 (JAG1). The combined AUC range in the training cohort was 0.898–0.959. However, in the IBS-D rat model, only JAG1 was significantly upregulated in colonic tissue, whereas CAT, ACADVL, CCL4, and CCNE1 showed no significant changes. Among the five markers, only JAG1 was significantly upregulated in the IBS-D rat colon, confirming its local gut relevance. CAT and CCNE1 showed strong diagnostic performance (AUC >0.9), whereas ACADVL and CCL4 performed modestly (AUC <0.7). Given the blood-derived QTL data and colonic validation, cross-tissue heterogeneity is a key caveat: JAG1 is robustly validated in colon, while the remaining four markers—especially ACADVL and CCL4—require further evaluation in blood, PBMCs, or other relevant tissues. Functional enrichment analysis revealed their involvement in critical biological processes, including oxidative stress, fatty acid metabolism, immune cell recruitment, cell cycle progression, and epithelial-immune crosstalk via Notch signaling. Immune infiltration analysis uncovered a distinct immune landscape in IBS, with significant correlations between biomarker expression and immune cell populations. Notably, only JAG1 was significantly upregulated in the colonic tissues of the IBS-D rat model, confirming its relevance to gut pathophysiology. No significant changes were detected for CAT, ACADVL, CCL4, or CCNE1 in the same tissue samples, highlighting the tissue-specific nature of these candidate biomarkers. The SMR analysis demonstrated consistent causal directions between genetically predicted expression and disease risk for these five markers, with no discordance relative to their upregulation in IBS patients. All biomarker validation was performed at the transcriptomic level (RT−qPCR); no protein−level assays (e.g., Western blot, IHC, or ELISA) were conducted. Conclusions This study delineates the genetic architecture linking aging and immunity to IBS through an integrative multi−omics and machine learning approach, providing novel putatively causal evidence and identifying JAG1 as a robustly validated biomarker with diagnostic and therapeutic potential. All QTL data were derived from blood or plasma samples. Candidate genes were identified through integrative multi-omics analysis, followed by functional annotation, machine learning-based feature selection, immune infiltration profiling, and drug-target prediction. The expression of key biomarkers was validated using reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) in colonic tissues from a rat model of diarrhea-predominant IBS (IBS-D). Results Integrative multi-omics analysis initially identified 34 high-confidence candidate genes. <title>Unveiling the aging-immune axis in irritable bowel syndrome: a multi-omics and machine learning approach to biomarker discovery and validation</title>
<abstract>Background Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a prevalent functional gastrointestinal disorder with an elusive pathophysiology. All QTL data were derived from blood or plasma samples. Candidate genes were identified through integrative multi-omics analysis, followed by functional annotation, machine learning-based feature selection, immune infiltration profiling, and drug-target prediction. The expression of key biomarkers was validated using reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) in colonic tissues from a rat model of diarrhea-predominant IBS (IBS-D). Results Integrative multi-omics analysis initially identified 34 high-confidence candidate genes. Through multi-algorithm machine learning such as least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), support vector machine recursive feature elimination (SVM-RFE), and random forest, these candidates were refined to a core panel of five biomarkers: the antioxidant enzyme catalase (CAT), acyl-CoA dehydrogenase very long chain (ACADVL), chemokine (C-C motif) ligand 4 (CCL4), cyclin E1 (CCNE1), and Jagged canonical Notch ligand 1 (JAG1). These biomarkers demonstrated strong diagnostic performance for CAT, CCNE1, and JAG1 in the validation cohort (AUC: 0.935–0.951), while ACADVL and CCL4 showed only moderate diagnostic potential (AUC: 0.645–0.649). The combined AUC range in the training cohort was 0.898–0.959. However, in the IBS-D rat model, only JAG1 was significantly upregulated in colonic tissue, whereas CAT, ACADVL, CCL4, and CCNE1 showed no significant changes. Among the five markers, only JAG1 was significantly upregulated in the IBS-D rat colon, confirming its local gut relevance. CAT and CCNE1 showed strong diagnostic performance (AUC >0.9), whereas ACADVL and CCL4 performed modestly (AUC <0.7). Given the blood-derived QTL data and colonic validation, cross-tissue heterogeneity is a key caveat: JAG1 is robustly validated in colon, while the remaining four markers—especially ACADVL and CCL4—require further evaluation in blood, PBMCs, or other relevant tissues. Conclusions This study delineates the genetic architecture linking aging and immunity to IBS through an integrative multi−omics and machine learning approach, providing novel putatively causal evidence and identifying JAG1 as a robustly validated biomarker with diagnostic and therapeutic potential. <title>Identification and validation of novel risk genes for intervertebral disc disorder by integrating large-scale multi-omics analyses and experimental studies.</title>
<abstract>Introduction Although genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified multiple genetic loci linked to intervertebral disc disorder (IDD), their functional characterization remains largely unelucidated. We aim to leverage an integrative analytical pipeline to identify novel IDD risk genes from genetic associations and experimentally validate their functional roles. Methods We integrated transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS), proteome-wide association studies (PWAS), expression and protein quantitative trait loci (eQTL and pQTL) colocalization analyses to identify potential causal genes for IDD. Subsequently, human intervertebral disc (IVD) tissues spanning degeneration grades and an in vivo mouse IDD model were employed to functionally characterize candidate risk genes. Results Integrative analysis of TWAS and PWAS with colocalization studies identified 104 genes and 10 proteins exhibiting causal associations with IDD. The identified genes/proteins were enriched in extracellular matrix organization, cellular senescence and collagen formation. Crucially, TMEM190, CILP2, and FOXO3 were demonstrated consistent evidence across TWAS, two independent PWAS datasets, and corresponding colocalization analyses, with CILP2 emerging as a potentially druggable target. Differential expression analysis revealed significant upregulated TMEM190 and CILP2, along with downregulated FOXO3 during IVD degeneration. These results were subsequently confirmed at protein levels in clinical specimens. Mouse model experiments further established that down-regulation of CILP2 alleviated IDD progression. Discussion Collectively, this work provides an updated compendium of putative IDD risk genes and delineates pathogenic roles for TMEM190, CILP2, and FOXO3, providing a broad hint for further research on novel mechanism and therapeutic targets for IDD.</abstract>
</record>

not interpret the result as aging biology. An age-related disease alone does
not supply that interpretation. An explicit current-result comparison with
`healthy aging` or `normal aging` is the positive pattern above; a background
mention without such a comparison is not.

Use `no` only when a complete record has no positive pattern and age is only a
covariate, demographic/recruitment label, older cohort, developmental time,
age-related disease context, disease-model progression, or background; when it
concerns persistence or durability rather than aging; or when it only predicts
chronological age.

Disease survival or time-to-event is not longevity/aging unless the authors
frame it that way. An incidental named age-related disease/tumor feature, such
as an age-related mutational signature in an analysis where age is merely
adjusted for, does not make aging a study construct.

Use `unclear` only when an aging-linked proxy is named but its current analysis
is unresolved. Senescence-related gene labels without a measured senescent
state are `unclear`. A target described only as senescence-inducing,
senescence-associated, or senescence-related without a measured, compared,
induced, reversed, or targeted senescent state is also `unclear`. If aging is
not `yes`, set multi-omics to `not_assessed`.

4. `multiomics_status`

- `yes`: explicit completed current-report multi-omics/multiome/integrated
  omics claim, or at least two distinct broad molecular modalities.
- `no`: complete record clearly uses zero or one modality and makes no
  current-report multi-omics claim.
- `unclear`: attribution to the current report is unresolved.
- `not_assessed`: an upstream scope criterion was not positive.

Future or ongoing multi-omics does not count. Two GWAS traits or multiple
assays of one modality remain one. Clinical variables, imaging, flow
cytometry, and routine biomarkers are not separate molecular modalities.
Always return `omics_layers=[]`.
An empirical title where `multiomics`, `multi-omics`, or `multi-omic`
directly modifies the analyzed phenotype, exposure, signature, age, or
analysis is a current-report multi-omics claim and is `yes`, including
`Associations of Multiomics X with Y`. Exact layers remain a full-text task.
A derived omics-based score/index, including an epigenetic age, used only as a
benchmark, comparator, covariate, or validation target is not a molecular
modality unless its underlying molecular data are analyzed. Comparing a
clinical/LLM prediction with epigenetic-age values and separately identifying
proteomic biomarkers is not multi-omics unless those molecular layers are
analytically connected in the current report.

ATOMIC CAUSAL TABLE

Return completion and two route-relevant signals. Do not synthesize
`identification_status`; Python derives it after schema validation.

Review precheck: if the current report is explicitly a review, systematic or
scoping review, meta-analysis, evidence synthesis, editorial, or commentary
with no substantive original empirical biological analysis, set
`completed_current_report=no`, `applied_design_signal=no`, and
`directional_result_signal=no`. Stop the causal table. Review searches,
charting, synthesis, mechanistic titles/conclusions, and summarized effects
from included studies are not original current-report empirical results.

Resource precheck: if the current report is a data descriptor, cohort profile,
atlas/database, biobank, repository, or infrastructure description and only
reports recruitment, collection, profiling availability, resource contents,
goals, or future use, set both completion and applied-design signals to `no`.
Completed collection/profiling alone is not substantive biological analysis.

1. `completed_current_report`

- `yes`: completed current-report biological analysis, experiment, secondary
  analysis, or substantive results.
- `no`: review without original analysis, protocol, future proposal,
  method-only description, or no completed substantive analysis/results.
- `unclear`: completion by the current report cannot be resolved.

A truncated record is complete when its current-report title says an analysis
`reveals/identifies/finds` a result, or its fragment says `we
performed/analyzed/analysed/profiled` and names the analysis or result.

2. `applied_design_signal`

- `yes`: current report applies MR/IV/SMR; an assigned randomized or
  nonrandomized intervention with outcome contrast; direct molecular
  perturbation; explicit quasi/natural experiment; formal mediation; causal
  DAG; structural causal/equation model; or another explicitly directed model.
- `no`: complete report applies none of those designs.
- `unclear`: possible application by the current report is unresolved.

An explicit knockout, repair/target-deficient, transgenic, or engineered
molecular/genotype model with outcomes attributed to the altered target is
`yes` even without a stated control. Generic disease/senescence/age/state
profiling, risk-score regression, colocalization, WGCNA, co-expression,
CellChat, SCENIC, ordinary trajectory, and undirected networks are `no`.
Planned designs without completed analysis are `no`.
An infection or treatment shared by all comparator groups is not its own
intervention contrast. Longitudinal sampling around routine vaccination is
`no` unless the report explicitly analyzes an outcome contrast attributed to
vaccination versus a different exposure level, dose, time, or control. Generic
`genetic approaches` without a named instrument or perturbation are `no`.
Explicitly applied structural equation modelling is `yes`, including for a
null direct path.
A named gene-variant, knock-in, heterozygous mutant, or genotype-notation
model with analyzed outcomes is an engineered genotype for this rule, even
when it is a recognized disease model.
A naturally occurring human genotype-carrier group or case/control comparison
is not an engineered genotype and is `no` unless MR/IV, a natural or
quasi-experiment, or another qualifying design is explicit.
Secondary analysis or model application to completed CRISPR, knockout,
knockdown, or other perturbation-screen outcomes is `yes` when those outcomes
are used to identify target-level effects, interactions, or dependencies; the
current authors need not have generated the screen. An unused external-study
mention is `no`.
This perturbation-screen positive has precedence over negative path-model,
dependency-mapping, association, or prediction rules. Identifying
synthetic-lethal interactions using CRISPR screen data is always `yes`, even
when another application in the same report only maps associations.

3. `directional_result_signal`

Inspect completed current-report result clauses literally.

- `yes`: `X causes Y`; `X drives/drove/is driving/driving Y`; `X-driven Y`;
  `driver of`; `X mediates
  Y`; `Y is mediated by X`; `X-mediated Y`; `X propagates Y`; `X affects Y`;
  `X influences/may influence Y`; `X regulates Y`; `regulator of`;
  `effect/impact of X on Y`; asserted `causal
  effect/link/association/relationship` between named variables; named
  `causal risk/protective genes/factors`; `X protects Y by Z`; `Y requires X`;
  `protective effect of X against/for Y`;
  `Y depends/is dependent on X`; a current result indicating dependence of Y
  on X;
  or another explicit current-result mechanism connecting X to Y.
- `no`: no matching completed current-result assertion.
- `unclear`: matching wording exists but current-report attribution is
  unresolved.

Apply this lexically. Do not downgrade a match because the study is profiling
or observational. `X-mediated Y` and asserted causal associations in current
Results are always `yes`. A signature/profile `revealed` or `linked` without a
listed directional assertion is `no`. A bare/truncated `causal role(s) of ...`
noun phrase without a result predicate is `no`.

A current Results clause stating that an analysis or exploratory network
`suggests/suggested X-mediated regulation` is `yes`. Tentative or exploratory
modifiers make it hypothesis-level but do not negate the literal match.
Explicit current-result change verbs are also `yes`: X
increases/decreases/enhances/reduces/inhibits/induces/prevents/accelerates/
slows/shortens/extends/alters Y, including inflected past-tense forms.
`Age-driven shifts` is an X-driven-Y match. A truncated
`multi-omics reveals that X drives Y` construction is attributed to the
current report, not marked unclear.
Current-result `genes/molecules driving these pathways` is also an
X-driving-Y match.

The change-verb rule requires a named acting X or manipulated exposure and a
named outcome Y. `Y increased in group A`, `Y decreased in tissue B`, or a
higher/lower case-control profile is descriptive and is `no` by itself.
Every listed directional verb includes its ordinary inflections and
participles when acting X and outcome Y remain explicit, including `causing`,
`driving`, `mediating`, `regulating`, `affecting`, and `influencing`.
Minor grammar errors do not negate an otherwise explicit X-to-Y assertion.
`Impact of X on Y`, including `global impact`, and `X is causally associated
with Y` are always `yes` when stated as current results.
`Protective effect of X against/for Y` in a current
Results/Findings/Conclusion sentence is always `yes`, including when the new
result identifies a mechanism involved in an already recognized protective
effect.
`Alterations/reorganization of X-mediated pathways` uses
`X-mediated pathways` as a pathway-class label and is `no` unless another
current-result clause states that X mediates a named outcome.
A current-result `X-mediated phenotype`, activation, regulation, or
inflammation phenotype is `yes`; it is not the pathway-class exception.

The causal review precheck also covers News & Views, research highlights, and
news items that summarize a named other study; their directional summaries
are `no`.
However, a report whose title says review but whose abstract states that the
authors performed a new public-data/bioinformatics analysis and presents its
own substantive or numerical Results has original current-report analysis;
assess those results normally.

Python derives retention status from completion and the two signals using the

- Preserve exposure/intervention, comparator, outcome, and estimand/contrast

  settled.
- `insufficient_title_abstract`: at least one scope criterion, completion
  value, or causal signal remains unclear.
- `conflict_unresolved`: the record itself contains irreconcilable evidence,
  not merely reviewer disagreement.
